title: Amateur Codes and Other Locks
bigQuestion: How did rules about pay, work, sex and race decide who was allowed to compete, and how were those doors opened?

story.title: One Question on a Form
story.kicker: An old entry form asks one question about money, and the answer decides who may run.
paragraphs: Lena finds a copy of an old athletics entry form in a library book about sport in Victorian England. The form asks for a name, a club and an event. Then it asks one more question. Has the athlete ever run for money, or for a money prize?

Her teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, explains that the question worked like a gate. An amateur could enter. A professional, someone who had been paid for sport, could not. Some early English rules went even further and shut out anyone who worked with their hands for a living.

Lena thinks about who worked with their hands in the 1860s. Bricklayers. Dockworkers. Miners. Factory hands. "So the rule was about jobs, not only money," she says. Mr. Adeyemi nods. "A wealthy young man could train all week for free. A mill worker lost a day's pay for every day he trained."

"When you study a rule like this," he says, "write down the rule first. Then write the names of people it kept out. Then find the year the door opened." Lena draws three columns on her paper: Rule, Who was shut out, Year it changed.
story.think: Who could afford to be an amateur when sport paid nothing and training took time away from work?

lessons.title: The Mechanics Clause
lessons.mainIdea: Early English amateur rules shut out manual workers, not only people who had been paid.
reading: In 1866 the Amateur Athletic Club was founded in London. It held championships in running, jumping and throwing. Its rules said an *amateur* must never have competed for money. They also shut out anyone who was a "mechanic, artisan or labourer."

That part became known as the *mechanics clause*. An *artisan* is a skilled worker who makes things by hand, such as a carpenter. A mechanic or labourer also worked with their hands for wages. Under the clause, a bricklayer could never count as an amateur, even if he had never been paid to run.

In 1880 a new national body, the Amateur Athletic Association, was founded at Oxford. It dropped the mechanics clause for running and jumping. Its rule asked only whether an athlete had been paid. Some rowing bodies kept manual-work rules for decades longer.

words.d: an athlete who has not been paid for sport; some old rules also required that they not work with their hands
a rule that barred manual workers from amateur competition
a skilled worker who makes things by hand

lessons.title: A Bricklayer at Henley
lessons.mainIdea: In 1920 John B. Kelly, a Philadelphia rower who had worked as a bricklayer, was refused entry at Henley, then won Olympic gold.
reading: The *Henley Royal Regatta* is a rowing event held each summer on the River Thames at Henley, England. It began in 1839. For many years, its entry rules kept out men who had worked with their hands.

*John B. Kelly* was a rower from Philadelphia. As a young man he worked as a bricklayer in his family's building business. In 1920 he entered the Diamond Sculls, Henley's top race for single rowers. His entry was refused.

The reasons were argued about. Henley pointed to an earlier ban on his club, the Vesper Boat Club of Philadelphia. Many people believed his work as a bricklayer was the real reason. American newspapers told the story widely.

That August, Kelly won the single sculls at the Olympic Games in Antwerp, Belgium. He beat Jack Beresford of Britain, who had won the Diamond Sculls that summer. On the same day, Kelly also won the double sculls with his cousin Paul Costello.

words.d: a yearly rowing event on the River Thames in England, begun in 1839
a Philadelphia rower and former bricklayer who won two Olympic golds in 1920
an event made up of boat races

look.title: One Summer, Two Results
look.text: Early summer 1920: Kelly's entry for the Diamond Sculls at Henley is refused. Jack Beresford wins the Diamond Sculls. August 1920: Kelly beats Beresford for the Olympic single sculls title in Antwerp.
look.prompt: What does the Olympic result suggest about whether Henley's entry rules measured skill?

choices: it was accepted, and he won

check.why: Kelly had worked as a bricklayer, and Henley's rules long kept out manual workers.

check.why: Kelly beat Beresford, the 1920 Diamond Sculls winner, in Antwerp.

lessons.title: Broken Time and a Rugby Split
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 northern English rugby clubs broke away so they could pay working players for wages lost while playing.
reading: In England the Football Association allowed professional players in 1885. Many soccer players in northern mill towns were factory workers. From then on, clubs could pay them openly. Rugby took a different path.

Rugby's *governing body*, the Rugby Football Union, kept strict amateur rules. Many northern rugby players worked in mills and mines. They lost wages when they missed a Saturday shift to play. Clubs wanted to pay them for this *broken time*, money to replace lost wages. The Union said no.

On August 29, 1895, more than twenty clubs met at the George Hotel in Huddersfield. They formed the Northern Rugby Football Union. It later became the Rugby Football League, and its game became known as *rugby league*. The older game is called rugby union.
The split lasted a century. Rugby union stayed officially amateur until August 1995. That year its world body, then the International Rugby Football Board, opened the game to professionals.

words.d: the organization that writes and enforces a sport's rules
money paid to replace wages a player lost while playing
the rugby game of the clubs that split away in 1895

lessons.title: Jim Thorpe's Medals
lessons.mainIdea: Jim Thorpe won two Olympic titles in 1912, lost them in 1913 under amateur rules, and was fully restored as champion in 2022.
reading: *Jim Thorpe* was a Sac and Fox athlete, born in 1887 in Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. He attended the *Carlisle Indian Industrial School* in Pennsylvania. The U.S. government ran Carlisle to separate Native children from their languages and cultures. Thorpe starred there in football and track.

At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm, Sweden, Thorpe won both the pentathlon and the decathlon. Each is a contest made up of several track and field events. Newspapers called him one of the greatest athletes in the world.

In January 1913 a newspaper reported news about Thorpe's past. He had played minor league baseball in North Carolina in 1909 and 1910 for small pay. Under the amateur rules of the time, that made him a professional. The Amateur Athletic Union and the *International Olympic Committee* took away his medals and removed his results.
Thorpe died in 1953. In 1982 the IOC agreed to restore his medals, and replicas were given to his family in 1983. In July 2022 the IOC listed him again as the sole champion of both 1912 events.

words.d: a Sac and Fox athlete who won the 1912 Olympic pentathlon and decathlon
a U.S. government boarding school in Pennsylvania for Native children, open 1879 to 1918
the body that runs the modern Olympic Games, often called the IOC

check.why: In 2022 the IOC named Thorpe the sole 1912 champion in both events.

lessons.title: Brundage and the Strict Years
lessons.mainIdea: Avery Brundage led the IOC from 1952 to 1972 and enforced strict amateur rules, which critics said were unequal.
reading: *Avery Brundage* competed in track and field at the 1912 Stockholm Games, the same Games as Thorpe. He later led American amateur sport. From 1952 to 1972 he was president of the International Olympic Committee.

Brundage believed the Olympics should be for amateurs only. Strict rules had already cost stars their places. In 1932 Finland's great distance runner Paavo Nurmi was barred from the Los Angeles Games. Officials ruled he had taken too much money for travel expenses.

At the 1972 Winter Games in Sapporo, Japan, the IOC barred Austrian skier Karl Schranz. Brundage pushed for the decision because Schranz had appeared in advertising. Schranz was sent home before the Games began.

Critics pointed to a *double standard*, one rule applied unequally to different people. Wealthy athletes could train full-time without pay. Some countries gave athletes government or army jobs while calling them amateurs. Athletes from working families often could not afford to train at all.

words.d: an American official who was IOC president from 1952 to 1972
a rule applied unequally to different people
an athlete who is paid for sport

look.prompt: Is the rule fair to all three athletes? Explain your answer using the term double standard.

lessons.title: The Doors Open to Professionals
lessons.mainIdea: From 1968 on, tennis and then the Olympics opened to professional players.
reading: Tennis had its own split. Top players who turned professional could not enter Wimbledon or the other major championships. In April 1968 the first open tournament was held in Bournemouth, England. Wimbledon opened to professionals that summer. This began the *Open Era*.

The IOC loosened its rules after Brundage retired in 1972. In the 1980s it began letting each sport's *international federation*, its world governing body, decide who could compete. Tennis returned to the Olympics in 1988 in Seoul, with professionals welcome.

In 1989 FIBA, the international basketball federation, voted to allow professional players in its events. At the 1992 Games in Barcelona, the United States sent NBA stars. Newspapers called the team the "Dream Team."

Rules about who may enter did not disappear. They became *eligibility* rules about age, school, residence and pay. In Illinois, the IHSA, founded in 1900, writes eligibility rules for high school sport.

words.d: the period in tennis since 1968, when amateurs and professionals play the same tournaments
the world governing body for one sport
the rules about who may enter or play

lessons.title: Women at the Early Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Women were kept out of the first modern Olympics in 1896 and were added to the Games slowly, event by event.
reading: At the ancient Olympic Games in Greece, married women were barred even from watching, according to the Greek writer Pausanias. Women at Olympia had their own festival, the *Heraia*, in honor of the goddess Hera. Pausanias described foot races for unmarried girls there.
*Pierre de Coubertin* of France founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894. He opposed women competing in the Games. No women competed at the first modern Olympics, held in Athens in 1896.

Women first competed at the 1900 Games in Paris, in a few sports such as tennis and golf. Charlotte Cooper of Britain won the tennis singles. She became the first woman to win an Olympic event on her own.

Women's track and field joined the Games in 1928 in Amsterdam. After the women's 800 meters that year, officials and newspapers claimed the race was too hard for women. The IOC dropped it. The women's 800 meters did not return until 1960.

words.d: an ancient festival at Olympia in honor of Hera, with races for girls
the Frenchman who founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894

lessons.title: A Race Number in 1967
lessons.mainIdea: Women ran the Boston Marathon without permission in 1966 and 1967, and Boston officially opened to women in 1972.
reading: The Boston Marathon began in 1897. A *marathon* is a road race of 26.2 miles. For its first seventy years, only men could enter Boston. In 1966 *Bobbi Gibb* hid near the start and ran the race without a number. She finished ahead of many of the men.

In 1967 *Kathrine Switzer* entered using the name "K. V. Switzer." She received an official race number. During the race, the official Jock Semple tried to pull her number off. Photographs of the moment ran in newspapers around the world. Switzer finished the race.

The Boston Marathon officially opened to women in 1972. The women's marathon was added to the Olympic Games in 1984 in Los Angeles. Joan Benoit of the United States won that first Olympic women's marathon.

lessons.title: A Written Clause in Golf
lessons.mainIdea: From 1934 to 1961 the PGA of America's rules limited membership to white golfers.
reading: The *PGA of America* is the association of professional golfers in the United States. It was founded in 1916. In 1934 it added a rule limiting membership to white golfers. It became known as the *Caucasian-only clause*.

The clause kept Black golfers out of most PGA tournaments. *Charlie Sifford* was a Black golfer from Charlotte, North Carolina. He won the National Negro Open, run by the United Golfers Association for Black golfers, many times.

Black golfers, lawyers and California's attorney general challenged the clause. In November 1961 the PGA removed it. Sifford became a full PGA touring player. In 1967 he won the Greater Hartford Open.
Private clubs kept their own doors. Augusta National Golf Club in Georgia, home of the Masters tournament, admitted its first Black member in 1990. It admitted its first women members in 2012.

the PGA rule, from 1934 to 1961, that limited membership to white golfers
a Black golfer who joined the PGA tour after the clause ended and won in 1967

lessons.title: Tennis, Football and Basketball Doors
lessons.mainIdea: Black athletes built their own bodies and pushed open tennis, pro football and pro basketball between 1946 and 1957.
reading: Black tennis players built their own governing body. The *American Tennis Association* was founded in 1916. It held national championships for Black players. *Althea Gibson* won ATA titles before white tournaments let her in.

In 1950 Gibson became the first Black player to compete at the U.S. National Championships, at Forest Hills, New York. Former champion Alice Marble had written a public letter urging officials to invite her. In 1957 Gibson won both Wimbledon and the U.S. title.

Professional football had some Black players in its early years. Fritz Pollard played and coached in the league in the 1920s. From 1934 through 1945, NFL teams signed no Black players. In 1946 the Los Angeles Rams signed Kenny Washington and Woody Strode.

The NBA's first Black players arrived in 1950. The Boston Celtics drafted Chuck Cooper. The New York Knicks signed Nat "Sweetwater" Clifton. Earl Lloyd of the Washington Capitols played first, on October 31, 1950.

words.d: a tennis body for Black players, founded in 1916
the first Black player at the U.S. Nationals (1950) and a Wimbledon champion (1957)
